morsel-doc-explorations-preview.html:
← back to case study · live prototype →

Structural explorations

A retrospective comparison of four design decisions. Each section shows the earlier approach, the current choice and a question for future testing. All menu content is sample data.

AFeed information density

The original feed showed photos without labels. Comparing names and prices meant opening each dish.

A1 · Photo-only v3.1 choice

  • Scan: few visual elements; scanning speed untested
  • Decisions: name, price and distance need a tap each
  • A11y: weakest; image-only targets
  • Review: two dishes cannot be compared without opening both

A2 · Minimal overlay

$19
$15 · 1.4 mi
$17
$14 · 0.8 mi
  • Scan: small labels over the photos; scanning speed untested
  • Decisions: price in-feed, but no name; long names clip in a glass pill
  • A11y: text on photos needs contrast testing

A3 · Text beneath v3.2 choice

Margherita, BlisteredElder & Ash · Shaw$19 · 0.4 mi
Shoyu Ramen No. 4Paper Lantern · H Street$17 · 1.2 mi
  • Scan: more information to read; scanning speed untested
  • Decisions: complete; names wrap instead of clipping
  • A11y: descriptive button names; a separate Save control
  • Without a photo: the card still works

A4 · Reveal on hold

Shoyu Ramen
$17 · 1.2 mi
  • Scan: clean until invoked
  • Decisions: gated behind an undiscoverable gesture
  • A11y: requires an alternative to long-press and a visible cue
Review · v3.2

A3 in every grid. I added text below the photos so names, prices and distances stay visible. The larger cards show fewer dishes at once; the featured image still gives the food room. To test: can people compare options without opening each one?

BEntry model

What stands between a first-time visitor and food, and where do dietary settings go?

B1 · Calibrate first, skippable v3.1 choice

1 Welcome + location rationale
2 Taste taps (≥4) — or skip
3 Lifestyle + allergies
→ Feed
  • Two screens before food; skip mitigates
  • Asked for a device location it could not use
  • Taste taps looked mandatory even when they weren't

B2 · Browse first

1 Welcome → straight to feed
2 Taste inferred silently from saves and opens
! Allergies asked at first save — late
  • Zero friction
  • Inference is opaque; hard to trust or correct
  • An allergic diner browses with no way to say so until later

B3 · Area, then optional dietary step v3.2 choice

1 Welcome names the demo area — nothing requested
2 Dietary settings — skip, always in Profile
→ Feed
Taste lives in Profile: "Tune"
  • Dietary settings offered before food, not forced
  • Nothing pretends to know the device location
  • Taste is a boost you can add, not a gate
Review · v3.2

B3. Dietary settings are offered before browsing and can be skipped. Taste preferences moved to Profile, where they can be added later. The welcome screen names the demo area instead of asking for device location. To test: can people start browsing and find these settings when they need them?

CEvidence on the dish page

v3.1 asked how a repeat-order percentage should present to be believed. The review asked a prior question: can the prototype produce that number at all?

C1 · Percentage alone

94% ordered again within 90 days
  • Unanchored: 94% of what?
  • Reads like marketing

C2 · % + sample + method v3.1 choice

94% ordered again within 90 days
131 verified diners · how we know
  • Clearer wording, but still no real order data
  • Needs order attribution, consent, a follow-up window and item identity across menu changes; none exist

C4 · Cold start v3.1 choice

NEW
New — no score yet
too few repeat orders
  • Admitting "not enough data" was right
  • There was no order data for any of the dishes

C5 · Facts with their basis v3.2 choice

Price$32Tax, tip and extras not included
Distance0.9 mi from ShawStraight-line, not a travel time
On the menuListedNot a promise it is available tonight
IngredientsMenu lists shellfishNot preparation or shared surfaces
  • Price, distance, menu status and listed ingredients, each with what it does not cover
  • The repeat-order percentage is removed; no dates imply a verification that never happened

Each card shows a photo, dish name, restaurant, neighborhood, menu price and distance. Images use a 4:5 ratio and names can wrap. Missing prices read "Price not listed". The same card is used in the feed, search and saves. Price is the listed menu price only. Distance is straight-line miles from Shaw, never a walk time. The card is one button whose accessible name reads the dish, restaurant, price, distance and any state chip. Save is a sibling control with aria-pressed, never nested. Without a photo the card is still complete.

State chip v3.2

Three states, one vocabulary
! Lists nuts? Ingredients unknownNo longer on menu
Marks a dish on a memory or context surface (saves, collections, restaurant menu) whose state needs attention: the menu lists an allergen the diner avoids; no ingredient information exists; the dish has left the menu. Recommendation surfaces never show the conflict chip, because conflicts are excluded upstream by the shared classifier. Top-left, kept clear of the save control. Use specific labels: "Lists nuts", "Ingredients unknown", "No longer on menu". Never "unsafe", never "safe". "!" for conflict, "?" for unknown, solid ink for unlisted: each state carries a glyph or treatment as well as a color. The chip text is part of the card's accessible name.

"Clear filters" clears browsing chips only. The same bar appears in search to show which filters are active. Allergy chips use the accent and the "!" glyph; nothing else on the bar does. Chips are buttons named "Browsing filter: within 1 mi. Edit" and so on. The bar is a labeled group.

Research plan

Three rounds, in order. Round A asks whether the problem is real before anyone reacts to screens. Round B tests the v3.2 flow with neutral tasks on the wireflow. Round C is a separate, smaller comprehension round on the three dietary states, with people who manage food allergies. None of the rounds has been run; every findings table is intentionally empty. Participant counts are planning ranges for qualitative work, not statistical claims.

Round A — recent behavior and problem relevance

5–6 conversations, 30–40 minutes each

  • Recruit by behavior, not by an invented persona: people who recently chose an unfamiliar casual meal in a city they know, including some who started from a photo or a saved post and some who went straight to a maps or delivery app. Include one person who tried an alternative food app and stopped.
  • Friends can pilot the script; they should not be the only evidence.
  • No screens are shown. Ask about the last relevant decision, using a non-sensitive saved post or search if they are comfortable. Do not collect unrelated messages, precise home locations, or medical details. Consent for recording; notes are enough if they prefer.
  • Do not introduce allergies as the assumed problem. Ask broadly about constraints and follow what they mention.

Prompts

  1. "Tell me about the last time you wanted something to eat but didn't know where to get it."
  2. "What happened first? What did you open next?"
  3. "What were you trying to check at each step?"
  4. "Was there a dish or place you considered and then ruled out? Why?"
  5. "How did you know you had enough information to decide?"
  6. "Did you save anything? Have you gone back to it?"
  7. "When has your usual method worked well?"
  8. "What would make trying another app not worth the effort?"
Gate. Continue with "choose a dish soon" if several independent examples show a similar unresolved step between an appealing dish and a usable choice. Reframe toward save-and-retrieve if remembering is the stronger problem. Pause the direction if the main problem is fees, group coordination, reservations, or menu accuracy this scope cannot address. A preference for attractive screens is not demand evidence.

Round B — information architecture and usability

5–6 moderated sessions, 35–45 minutes each

  • Likely users from Round A's profile, fresh where possible. Their own phone if they have one.
  • Open with a neutral statement: the catalog is simulated, the restaurants are fictional, and nothing can be ordered. Then let them choose their path; think aloud; never name the intended button.
  • Record for each task: completed unaided / completed with help / not completed; the actual obstacle; the information used. Task time is diagnostic only.
#Task (read aloud)What to observeDesign decision it informs
1"You want dinner soon near the demo area. Pick something you would consider, keeping the menu price within $20."feedWhat they notice, how they narrow, whether they compare without opening every cardCard content and information order
2"You're in the mood for noodles. Find an option you would consider, then look at another and go back."searchQuery and constraint retention, comparison, backtrackingSearch and navigation state
3"You can't decide yet. Keep two options somewhere you can find them later."saveDiscovery of Save; whether collections help or interruptSave interaction and saved-card content
4"Now you're ready to get one of them. Show me what you would do next."next stepExpected destination; menu versus checkout; whether they believe an order happenedNext-step sheet and handoff copy
5"This one isn't available in this scenario. What would you do?"off the menuContext retention and recovery without starting overUnavailable-item handling
6"You want to look at another area."areaUnderstanding of demo coverage; no belief that the app is brokenArea and not-covered state
Follow-ups, always non-leading: "What did you expect to happen?" · "What would you do next?" · "You hesitated there — what were you weighing?" Never: "Did you like…", "Wasn't that easy?" With a fictional catalog this round tests comprehension and interaction. It cannot show that someone would buy a dish, trust the catalog, or stop using another app.
Gate. Any belief that an order was placed, that a device location was detected, or that missing ingredient information means the dish is fine is a critical comprehension issue. Fix repeated decision barriers before polishing secondary screens.

Round C — dietary information comprehension

3–4 sessions with people who manage a food allergy, plus a domain reviewer if one is available

  • Test how the information is understood. Do not ask anyone to order or eat based on the prototype.
  • Fixtures: a listed conflict, a dish with no ingredient information, a saved conflict, a related-dish route, and a restaurant page showing flagged dishes for context.
  • Collect the initial interpretation before explaining anything; then clarify the prototype's limits.
  • If no domain reviewer is available, keep the limitation and do not present the feature as validated.
#PromptWhat to observe
C1"What does this information tell you? What does it leave unanswered?"Whether "menu lists" is read as an ingredient claim only, not a preparation claim
C2"Why do you think this item is or isn't in these results?"Whether the listed-apart section is understood as "unknown", not "fine" or "bad"
C3"What would you need to check before making a decision?"Whether "check with the restaurant" is a plan or a shrug
C4"What do you expect this next step to do?"Whether the handoff is read as leaving the app, not as ordering
Gate. If the information repeatedly reads as a guarantee, reduce the feature's claim and scope. More disclaimers are not the answer. The wording under test: Morsel excludes dishes whose menu lists an avoided ingredient, sets aside dishes with no ingredient information, and never calls anything safe.

Severity scale

  • S1 — trust or comprehension breach: the diner believes an order was placed, a location was detected, or missing information means the dish is fine. Fix before anything else.
  • S2 — task blocker: cannot complete a core task (compare, save, hand off) without moderator help.
  • S3 — friction: completes with detours, misclicks, or visible hesitation.
  • S4 — polish: cosmetic or preference-level.

Findings → iteration matrix

Finding (evidence)SessionsSeverityHypothesisDesign responseStatus
Fill after sessions — one row per distinct finding, merged across participants. Report counts with context ("three of five missed the price"), never small-sample percentages.

Before / after template

For each S1–S2 finding that changes the design, produce one pair for the case study:

  1. Before: the v3.2 state and the one-line finding, with the count.
  2. After: the revised state, what changed, and why it addresses the evidence.
  3. Verdict line: the re-test criterion.

Identical crop and zoom for both frames so the change reads instantly. Retrospective design-review pairs (the v3.1 → v3.2 changes) stay labeled as review, not as findings.

No sessions have been run. The case currently documents a design review. This research would help assess whether the changes are useful to people choosing a meal.
